utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. As you can see, only two Judges are present today. Judge Nyambe is not able to attend because of another commitment. The Chamber decided to sit with two Judges, pursuant to Rule 15 bis. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Sit down, please. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. Mr. McCloskey has additional questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honour, Judge Mindua, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we should go where we left off, which was P1214. And if we could be in page 8 in English and page 13 of the B/C/S. And if we'll recall, this is the Directive for Upcoming Operations 7. And, General, I just -- we've talked a bit about which branches or which people have contributed to various parts of this document. Now we see the section entitled "Unit Assignments," and then it starts with the Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps, and then works its way through the corps. Can you tell us, who or which branches would have provided the information that directs these -- the corps regarding these various military objectives?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Administration for Operations and Education, as well as the Organ for Branches, follow and monitor the situation in the units, the level of their manning, and the chief of the administration gives the proposal for the use of his own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that the chief of the Administration of Operations and Training would be the one drafting these -- this information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He proposes the engagement of his own forces, which means the troops, the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So at -- for this directive, that would have been General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the actual wording in this, could that be changed by the president or another -- General Tolimir, General Mladic, another senior officer, could they offer languages for this draft before it's actually sent to the president for his review and signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the administration gives this proposal to the Chief of Staff; if not him, then the commander. The commander can then adopt it fully, partially, or after some corrections have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So is it fair to say that while General Miletic drafts most of this, that it's impossible to tell precisely which person drafted an individual sentence or section?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for the use of the troops is provided by the chief of the administration. Whether the superior to whom he submits his proposal will make changes or whether he will fully adopt the proposal depends on the moment, the conditions, and the way of thinking on the part of the superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go over a couple of pages to the Drina Corps section, which should be, in Serbian, page 15. It should be page 10 in the English. And we've all seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I -- so in concentrating on the Drina Corps, the first part of it talks about: "Enemy breakthroughs along the selected operative-tactical lines should be prevented by extremely persistent and active defence in co-operations with part of the forces of the SRK on the north-west part of the war front and around the enclaves. As many enemy forces as possible should be tied down by diversionary and active combat operations on the north-west part of the front ..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "North-west," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: " ... using operational and tactical camouflage measures ..." And this is the part I call your attention to: "... while in the direction of Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Now, my first question is: Now, I know you weren't there and didn't take part in this drafting, but do you know, from gaining knowledge after the fact, who actually wrote out this section: "... by planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa"? Do you know who actually wrote that in there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never came by information as to who composed that part or that particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the next sentence: "In case the UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the Drina Corps shall plan an operations named Jadar, with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves and definitively liberating the Drina Valley region." Can we read this to mean that there would not be an operation to take out the enclaves until the UNPROFOR forces left, back when they were signing this in March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what estimates were used in order to foresee the departure of UNPROFOR. I suppose that this is based on some intelligence, some information, but I don't know whose, because UNPROFOR and its status and its stay in the area were all a matter of politics and agreements which were reached at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to greet everybody present in the courtroom. May God's peace reign in this house, and may God's will be done in these proceedings, and not necessarily mine. Your Honours, this witness did not participate in the drafting of the directive. He just threw a perfunctory glance at it. And now he's being asked to speculate. He is asked to provide desirable answers on something that he doesn't know because he never participated in that. Please bear that in mind. The witness did not participate in the drafting of this directive. He didn't write it. He said he didn't know. So I'm sure that he doesn't know anything about the case of departure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we heard the answer of the witness, that he doesn't know anything, who drafted this part of the Directive 7. However, we have seen in this court so many documents where both parties put questions to the witnesses of their understanding of the document, and this is exactly what Mr. McCloskey did with this witness now, asking about his understanding of this document as an insider, as a person who was taking -- was a member of the relevant army. So I don't see that point. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may I just respond briefly, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tolimir should add something, and then you may respond.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to you. The interpretation was of Mr. McCloskey's words as to who wrote this. This is how -- the interpretation that I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps he didn't get the question. That was: Did you learn, after you returned, who wrote this, which is what I actually said. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You received an answer, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And just to correct the record -- well, I can ask the witness on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, this directive was -- included the operations for the time-frame that would have applied to you after your return to the Main Staff, would it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you retrieved this from the strong-box and read it, did it have any application to you at the time of what your supreme commanders might want to have in mind for the upcoming period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said that I threw just a perfunctory look at it. I did it discreetly, unbeknownst to Mr. -- to General Miletic. This is a lengthy document. I didn't have time to read all of it. I just leafed through it, I looked at some segments, and then I returned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to B/C/S page 19. It should be 14 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want to direct your attention to -- it's under the title "Support for Combat Operations: Moral and Psychological Support." And I want you to go down to paragraph 4, and it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, not paragraph 4, but the fourth paragraph under 6.1. It's the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go back, please? Please, could you read the beginning of what you want me to look at. The document has been moved to the following page, and I can see "Command and Control" there at the bullet point 7. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's not going to contain the part I want. It's going to be the fourth paragraph, so we need to go over to the next page. I think it is the --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- paragraph up. It begins: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR ..." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. "... and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Now, when you came back on the 17th, Srebrenica was gone, pretty much, as an enclave. Zepa was not receiving regular convoys; it was in a particular situation. So when you got back on the 17th, did you hear that this was a policy for any of the remaining enclaves, this restrictive -- unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits and the rest, how it states out as to do it as to limit the support, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't hear anybody talk about that in my presence. I did not read the entire document. I've not had the same opportunity as I have now. I just cast a perfunctory glance at it again. So I was not informed about this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you think of this? Is this professional -- is this a professional idea? Is it a professional direction? Is it proper?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can share with you my personal opinion. When there are conflicts, a lot of things happen. The entire states are blockaded for years, for 10 years. People suffer, unable to get supplies and to live normally. So from the humanitarian point of view, it's not proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think we should go to the last page in both. I think it's page 15 --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I am saying this in respect of civilians. However, when it comes to the enemy side, to the opposing side, then I think that this is not illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We need to go back, page 21 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I would agree with you. Siege warfare against -- is that what you're referring to? Siege warfare against an armed force, that it's completely legitimate to restrict food, supplies, armaments to the actual force? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. However, here we have a situation where an area is treated as a demilitarised zone, although there are forces of a division there and every day they inflict losses on the army, they plunder. Even before the month of June, before I came, nine sabotage terrorist groups were sent to the immediate vicinity of the Main Staff, and they inflicted losses on the Signals Regiment and the regiment that was providing security for the Main Staff. And allegedly that was done from the allegedly protected -- or, rather, allegedly demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know of those -- of some of those incidents, and I agree with you, General. And my question is: Does that conduct by the Muslim forces, in your training, justify the targeting of the civilians or the restriction of their humanitarian aid? Because the army is doing something like that that was wrong, under the UN rules, can the Serb Army take that out on the civilians?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not towards the civilians. But in Republika Srpska, we were under an embargo, and the entire population in the territory of Republika Srpska suffered due to the blockade that was imposed. I'm not justifying what I read here with what had happened to us, but things happen. The treatment is not even-handed towards everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'm done with that. And given that last -- well, that last paragraph -- sorry, that came under the Morale and Legal Section. That would be General Gvero's section; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Sector for Morale, Religious, and Legal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before we leave, as promised, we do now see the last page and the name of the supreme commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic, who you've talked about, typed by Sergeant Spasoja Zeljkovic. Did Zeljkovic work in Operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember where Zeljkovic worked?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was in the Logistics Sector. He was employed on the computer data entry details. I think that this was done by computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And while we're on a simple point, you mentioned one of the officers in the Main Staff as a Nikola Trkulja. Does "Nedjeljko Trkulja" ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke when I said that name. I was wrong. His name is Nedeljko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his position, again?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Trkulja was in the Organ for Branches, and he was the chief of the Armoured Mechanised Units Branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. And you've spoken briefly now about the Main Staff, about the Operations Branch and the Chief of Staff. Can you tell us, again briefly, what are the basic jobs of the assistant commander? I don't want to hear about intel and security and logistics. But, fundamentally, they're not commanders, they're assistant commanders. What is their basic responsibility in this Main Staff, in very simple terms?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you have in mind, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No one in particular, but just generally. What does this commander share, what does his -- we know that they are at the head of specific branches, but what is their basic job in relation to the commander who they are assisting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They represent the inner command, the inner circle of the command. In the absence of the commander himself, one of them, appointed by the commander, stands in for him or deputizes for him while he's absent, in terms of co-ordination and supervising the work of the Main Staff Command and the units as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do they ever offer proposals or advice to the commander on their particular area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the commander requests advice or opinion from a sector, that sector will provide their estimate or a position with regard to a problem. And there is discussion about important issues. He will probably want to hear their opinion, and he will want to hear their proposals as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if General Mladic hears the proposal of, well, let's say of General Gvero and issues an order pursuant to that proposal, does General Gvero have responsibility regarding the overseeing or monitoring of that order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can receive reports about things and be up to date with regard to the implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What are his responsibilities regarding the implementation, and the commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that the proposal was received from a certain officer doesn't necessarily mean that implementation follows. The commander may assign somebody else to oversee the implementation of that task. It depends on the nature of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You talked briefly about the -- I believe it was the job of civil --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 12, lines 4 through 7, I believe that the witness's words were not very faithfully recorded. I believe that the witness spoke not only about the nature of the task but also about the size of the task, and there are also some other inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, we can't check that. We have to rely on the interpretation and the record. We can follow in English but not in B/C/S. It is always helpful not to speak too fast, what you did just now. We have to -- that may be checked later, in comparison with the tape in B/C/S. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm happy to check that -- the tape on that, Mr. President, so we'll try to add that, and we'll work with Mr. Gajic on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time I would put one question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the reason why these officers are called assistant commanders? What is the meaning of the word "assistant"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a group of officers who are charged with some tasks in their sectors, but they are immediately subordinate to the commander and they make up the inner circle of the command. If a problem arises, and let's take that there are three assistants, no matter where exactly the problem lies, the commander will ask everyone to hear their opinion with regard to the solution to the problem. If the original proposal was mine, I'm not necessarily the one to monitor the implementation of the task because the commander can adopt somebody else's proposal and not necessarily the proposal of the one who's in charge of the issues with -- the matters to which the task pertains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understood you in the following way: Is the group of assistant commanders a kind of a collegium or a team? Is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And one of these assistant commanders is the deputy of the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this was, in this case, General Milovanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it happen that one of the other assistant commanders stand in for the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How could that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Chief of Staff is temporarily absent and the commander has to go away too, then he will select one of the assistants present to stand in for him and the commander while he's away. And during that time, that person will have the same powers as the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means the commander would appoint one of his assistants to stand in for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us just a brief idea of the authority of an assistant commander? For example, would he normally be able to issue orders to anyone he wants?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he doesn't have those rights. He can only issue orders in the spirit of the basic decisions adopted by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can he issue orders to his subordinates, like you've talked to us before about General Miletic had a few subordinates?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can. Miletic can issue orders from his remit, that is, to me and Colonel Djeric. That's the regular daily work. And the assistant commander, if authorised to co-ordinate in the Command of the Main Staff, then he could also co-ordinate some tasks between the sectors and administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And now when an assistant commander gets appointed by Mladic as the person in charge, because Mladic is gone and Milovanovic is gone, now what powers of order does that person have, the one who is now in charge in the absence of Mladic and Milovanovic? Can he now issue orders, basically, in a different way than you've described?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the relations are there. But I must return to the first thing. Orders can be -- can only be -- can only go as far as the framework laid down by the commander while he was there. But the periods of time when you stand in for the commander and act on his behalf are short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think we may get some examples that may help us with that. Let me now go to -- you've talked briefly about Colonel Djeric's position, and I think we've referred to it as the Department of Civil Affairs, and you've described that briefly. Can you tell us just a little bit about the process where UNPROFOR or humanitarian organisations would request convoy clearance? Who would they request those clearances from? Who would handle them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must first correct you. You mentioned Colonel Djeric. You probably meant Colonel Milos Djurdjic, who was chief of the Department for Liaison with International Military Representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I apologise. Colonel Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All requests were received by fax in the department headed by Djurdjic. Upon receiving such requests, Colonel Djurdjic processed them, marked them, and so on, and turned them into proposals to the commander. And he took them to the commander for approval. It was up to the commander to approve these requests or not to approve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And once a request was approved or not approved, did the Operations Branch get involved?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjevic [as interpreted] would draft a notification to the units through whose zone the convoys would travel and who manned the check-points along that route. He would integrate all these requests into one document, and this document, when it was typed, he would submit to General Miletic for signature; if he was absent, then to his Chief of Staff. Such authorisations were most frequently signed either by the Chief of Staff or the by the chief of the Operations and Training Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I clarify the transcript. Page 16, line 7. At the beginning of your last answer, you are recorded to having referred to Colonel Djurdjevic. Is that correct? Or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And not Colonel Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And not Colonel Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I said "Djurdjevic," but I meant the chief of the Department for Liaison with International Military Representatives, and he was Colonel Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation. These names are quite similar and everybody is in a position to make a mistake. I don't know if you misspoke or the interpreter misspoke. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to an example of some convoy materials. Let's go to 65 ter 6022, which is a document you'll recall seeing in the last trial. And as we just take a look at this to get oriented, we'll see in the English that this is dated in June. It says, 1995, and it's from Major General Nicolai of the BH Headquarters. And it's requesting a approval for a convoy of -- for medical evacuation. And if we look over and see the original document, we can see some handwriting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 5062 now. But leave the English up. Excuse me, 5260. And can we blow the B/C/S version up. We don't need the English version because it's on the right. No, maybe we can't do that. Well, it's all right, we can do it this way. We'll use the old exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The blue writing on the top, did you do that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date and the signature, "14 November 2008, Ljubomir Obradovic," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's when you testified and made these other markings on the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We see two red circles. One is marked with the number 1 on the far right. What is -- what have you circled there in number 1? What is that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right, the initials of General Tolimir. And there's a slash. And outside the red circle there's a struck-out "A/A."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we see that. What does that "A/A" mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To archive, to be archived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then how about the next circle with the red number 2 in it; what is that encircling? What do you identify, if anything, in there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I circled the initials of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, it's not exactly clear to us because we see some writing in there. Can you write on this document again and just put an arrow to where the actual initial of General Mladic is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, would it be possible to have the original document, without these markings by the witness in the prior trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can go back to it. It was the first one I put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was 65 ter 6022; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can see it more clear without the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, and I'll have him -- I'll ask him to do that, then. If we could go back to 6022. That's fine. And perhaps we can blow that up just a little bit in the area that we're talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you take the pen, and if you could, circle what you've concluded were the initials of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've circled including a very long vertical line next to the squiggles. Is that long vertical line part of the initials, in your knowledge, or was that something else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's just a slash, not part of the initial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's erase that, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just put a circle around what you -- the precise initials.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you mark that circle with an A.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you now circle, as precisely as you can, what you are concluding are General Mladic's initials.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you mark that with a B.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we see immediately above General Mladic's initials a word that is circled. Can you tell us what that word is that's circled in black?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the affirmative word "da" in Serbian, which means "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you circle the whole circle of the "da" and put C by that, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- thank you. Can you give us any idea why these initials are on here? First of all, let's start with General Mladic's. What's that mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that the commander reviewed this document when Colonel Milos Djurdjic brought it to him, that he approved it, wrote "Yes" on it, and confirmed or certified that with his initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then why would General Tolimir be initialling this document as well, as you've identified?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why there are the initials of General Tolimir here and whether they were placed there before or after the commander's initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall, in your prior testimony, talking about General Tolimir's involvement in this, or the Security Branch's?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that concerns the Security and Intelligence Sector because of our bad experience that we had with some convoys that transported undeclared goods and in some cases even ammunition and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So given the need to carefully monitor these convoys from contraband, was the Security Branch involved in this monitoring and this work, as we see General Tolimir is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent, but here, in this procedure of approving, I don't know why these initials are here. I can only make an assumption, namely that Djurdjic first took it to General Tolimir and suggested that it be archived, and maybe subsequently the commander approved it. And only then was this A/A mark placed here. But then these are my speculations. I can't know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2144, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is, of course, the marked versions as well as the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. Are you tendering also the original? We now received - this is my understanding - the document with the markings as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and the, of course, the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's just a good idea, to have both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The original without the markings by the witness, and this is 65 ter 6022.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2145, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about 65 ter 5260, which was the document with the previous markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think, for consistency, that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we go to 65 ter 5137. All right. I'm sorry, we need to go to 5211. No, sorry. We'll be there in a minute. I apologise. Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is still 65 ter 5137, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. And this is the correct document. They just were managed in a -- all right, and ... all right. So let's go back to the first page. I see where we're at now. And I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We can see here that this is a document from Miletic to the UNPROFOR, and it's noting that this convoy request is not approved. And we see it's in the name of Colonel Miletic. Can you read the actual signature in the stamped version? And I've got the original if you can't make that out.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surname is Pandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And that's -- you've mentioned Pandzic before. Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Colonel Radoslav Pandzic at the time in the airforce and anti-aircraft defence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And since we see Miletic's name on this, was this something -- I mean, we know you weren't there at this point - we can see it's 6 March - but would this be something that he was involved in at times, notifying UNPROFOR of convoy requests, declinations or approvals?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information written based on a decision by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we understand that. I'm just asking -- we see Miletic's name on the bottom of it. Would he normally be involved in notifying UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't something that was normally done. It was normally done by the Chief of Staff. But since he was absent, it was signed by Miletic. And Colonel Djurdjic, the person who actually drafted it, put down this signature block, and then it was Pandzic who signed it because he did not have the right to sign these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, please wait a moment. And we forgot something else. We have to come back to another document. Judge Mindua wanted to put a question to that after you had finished with this document. But I didn't understand this procedure of signature. We have in the English translation: "... for standing in for the Chief of Staff." In my understanding, the Chief of Staff was General Milovanovic. Standing in for him was his deputy, General Miletic, at that time perhaps Colonel Miletic. How was it possible that a third person could sign this document instead of Miletic? Or did I miss something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you didn't miss anything. It says: "Standing in for the Chief of Staff, Colonel Miletic." However, he was probably absent. So then for the person standing in, it was Colonel Pandzic who signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there -- do you see the word "za" there somewhere, so that it's clear that Pandzic is not trying to fake Miletic's signature, that he's saying "za" and then puts his own name? Can you see a "za" there? In -- on the stamp, do you see "za" anywhere? Just to help us sort out the process.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you circle again the "za" so that that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher. Wait a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Oh, you are already a professional in court procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We see the red circle, so I would offer this into evidence before I forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The marked document should be a document in our case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we go to another page in the document. It should be, in e-court, page 2. And for the English, we need to go to 0679-3609. And I have the original of this. As we can see, the black markings are very hard to make out on the screen. If I could ask the witness to take a look at the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please. And if it's possible to enlarge that part in the meantime, it would be helpful. I suppose, Mr. McCloskey, you will put questions in relation to the handwritten markings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just waiting for the English translation to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But are you able to make out the original, General, what it says in the handwritten part?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Toso," and that is underlined. "What do you think about the request?" And then it says: "Would it be possible to impose a condition, if we decide that in the end? Give your proposal." And then the initial of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can we blow up that handwritten section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was told we have a problem. The last marking, the word "za" was lost. It was not saved. And you may proceed. But come back to that to ask the witness to encircle this word again so that can be saved. I think we have not the right English version on the screen in relation to this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is correct. It should be on its way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was the ERN number 0679-3609, if that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But this can't be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I recall it, and I think the general's -- what he read is my recollection of what the translator saw. So I think from the transcript for now I know it's in there. I know it's not ideal, but if you remember what he said, that's pretty much what the translator saw as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A document with the ERN number you have given is not in e-court, I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It may be checked later. But if you're only dealing with this -- oh, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, there's tricky parts of e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is a different ERN number, I was told, but now we have it on the screen. This is helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thank everyone for their patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, could you just again circle what you recognise as General Mladic's initials?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, should we put only the B/C/S version on the screen and enlarge that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We don't need the English for the encircling, so that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, we didn't press the right button, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Although you are an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's another button that needs to get pressed, sir, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the Court Usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you very much. This should be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The marked document, I hope it is saved. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, as well, the underlying document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2149, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we better go back to "za" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- which is the same document, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need only the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get only B/C/S. Blow it up, please, a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, could you circle that "za" again. We've lost the -- ah, you've got the button figured out. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was already received and has a P number, but I hope it will be possible to save it. I was told we have, today, many problems with the saving of markings, which is very unfortunate. We should try to figure out what might be the reason during the break. Have you done everything with this document? We'll come back to that later to redo the marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I don't -- I just wanted to ask a few basic questions, so we should keep it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, General, we again, here -- who wrote the note directed to General Tolimir under the word "Toso"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So here again we see General Tolimir involved in a -- this is a medical evacuation related to Srebrenica. Would this have security implications as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, we should be more precise. How could we conclude on the basis of this that I was appraised of the medical evacuation? Maybe the witness should be asked whether this document bears any sign of my activity, any information of what I was doing at the time, or maybe this is merely an assumption on the part of Mr. McCloskey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if you can deal with this, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, let me ask you this: We just saw a similar document with General Tolimir's initials on it and next to General Mladic's initials, and now we see a document where General Mladic is asking General Tolimir for a proposal. When General Mladic takes a serious document like this and asked one of his assistant commanders for a proposal, does that get shown to the assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be necessary to see the document for which an opinion or proposal is sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page. It's the document you just looked at. It's the one that you have in front of you. You just -- you see it? I'm asking about this proposal, that it says: "Toso, give me your proposal about this." And it's on this medical evacuation. Would that be seen by General Mladic -- excuse me, by General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a way, he should tell him why he is requesting his proposal. Now, whether he told him about the contents of the document or whether he forwarded the document to him, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is: When General Mladic writes a note to General Tolimir or any other of his assistant commanders on an important document from UNPROFOR, should that note -- that handwritten original note that you have in front of you, should that be passed on to General Tolimir, or could it just get mislaid, or put someplace, or lost?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that this document actually reached General Tolimir. However, based on this, he was supposed to appraise himself of the contents of the document and then put forward the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try one more time, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- put a question. General Mladic wrote this note, as you told us. What was his expectation what will happen with this document after having made this note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was supposed to reach General Tolimir so that he can give the proposal in line with the question asked of him, because the administrative practice that we followed gives the possibility to an officer to make a short note on the margin of the document in which he either asks for a proposal or instructs the subordinates to carry out a certain tasks. Or to say, I approve this, or, I do not approve this. So it is possible to give a short instruction. And I think that this is exactly what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the person who receives this document with the handwritten note of Mladic was supposed to forward it to the relevant person, in this case to General Tolimir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This memo was taken to the commander by Colonel Djurdjic. Whether the commander wrote it at that time or later on, I don't know. But when it was returned, this document was supposed to come to General Tolimir so that he could give a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware at any time where General Tolimir ignored a request from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he knew about it or did not know about it. I'm not aware of that. Because this line goes from the commander, through Colonel Djurdjic, towards the chief of sector, so I cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, that wasn't my question. My question was more general, and that is: Were you ever familiar with a time -- was there ever a breakdown that you ever saw between General Mladic and General Tolimir where General Tolimir would ignore a specific proposal, any proposal, or any request for a proposal from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never present, I never had the possibility to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of any of the assistant commanders or the Chief of Staff ever ignoring General Mladic when he requests them to give him a proposal?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any time where any of the assistant commanders or the Chief of Staff ever did not follow out an order that Mladic gave them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that. I don't have information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So have you ever heard about it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my -- I can see that my time is almost out, and I'm -- this has been very difficult to judge, the time that this has taken, and I apologise for that. And I really don't want this witness to have to stay, but if I could -- if we could break now, I will try to go through my remaining materials, but I have significant materials. And I will try to get a better estimate, but this has just been - I apologise - very difficult. Perhaps I'm getting spoiled by 92 ter, but I've not given a good estimate. I don't think it should take more than one more session, but I can see one more session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the technical difficulties with the markings and the tendering of documents can't count against you and, therefore, I think we should proceed in the following way -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: During the break we should try to resolve the technical problems. After the break you should try to get the markings done again with the numbers we have already received. But before we break - we have several minutes left - I would like to go back to the Directive 7. That was P1214. The last page we saw - I don't know which one it was - Judge Mindua wants to put a question before the break. Let's see if we can get it back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Directive 7 is 1214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the English translation of the page. Yes, there it is. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. So we have Directive 7 in English and we see the page on the screen. Witness, I would just like to go back briefly to what was said earlier at page 10 of the transcript, starting at line 11, regarding the directive. At the bottom of the page, you have the words "Staff Sergeant Spasoja Zeljkovic." You said that this person worked at the Logistics Sector and that he worked at the Computer Data Department. So I would like to know: That department, or this sector, was it placed under the command of the supreme commander directly, or was it placed under the command of the commander of the Main Staff, or was it placed under the Administration of Operations and Education, led by General Radivoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Sergeant Zeljkovic was within the Logistics Sector. That sector is not directly subordinated to the supreme commander. It is only subordinated through the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you for this information. Now, I'd like to ask you this, because yesterday you explained to us that the drafting of the directive, the directive is the instrument of the command -- supreme commander, and it is the instrument of -- that they use. You told us the directive could be elaborated in two ways; there was a long method and a short method. The long method included the inputs stemming from all sectors and organs, and afterwards the document was signed by either the supreme commander or the staff commander, Main Staff commander. So my question is the following: After the inputs coming from lower organs to the supreme commander, after they have been drafted, if the commander -- the supreme commander wanted to add something or if he wanted to modify something, who is the person who was in charge of typing the directive before the supreme commander signs it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, who was in charge of entering the amendments that may have come from the supreme commander, I don't know whether there was a special person to enter those amendments and who was it who was doing that job in his cabinet. In this case, I think that it says that it was finalised by Staff Sergeant Spasoja Zeljkovic. And if you ask me about possible interventions, how they arrived, how they were typed, whether it was entered by hand and then later on sent for retyping and then resent for a signature, I wouldn't know the particulars of that process. I don't know what was the practice. These are the possibilities that I have outlined: The supreme commander would receive a typed document, he would look at it, enter comments in the margin about what needed to be amended or changed, and then he would return it for retyping. And that retyped version would then also include his amendments. In this case, it seems that the final version was typed by this Staff Sergeant Zeljkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. In fact, this document was drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic. This is clear. Then the document was typed by the sergeant whose name we see here. We don't really know if he was directly attached to the supreme commander or to Colonel Miletic. That's something we don't know from this document. But I don't really understand very clearly. Why do you have to put the name of the person who typed the document if, in the end, we don't know if any modifications were brought in and if he took -- if he took them into account when he typed the final document? Witness, I don't know if you understood my question. I am just trying to understand who is the person who, in the end, typed the final version of the document. This is why usually the initials of the person are put there. But according to your explanation it's very difficult to see who was the person who typed this final version; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me clear one thing first. Staff Sergeant Zeljkovic, in an organisational way, looking at the way the establishment was at the time, he belongs to the Logistics Support Sector. He is not in the sphere of the supreme commander. He is, in some way, indirectly subordinated to him through the commander of the Main Staff and the commander of the Logistics Sector. Why it was he who was engaged to enter those things, that I don't know. And what exactly happened, it's impossible for us to figure out. It's possible that, for instance, when he typed the first version, and then Colonel Miletic submitted it to the commander for signature, maybe if he had some amendments he could have written those amendments in pencil by hand on the paper and then returned the text to be retyped. And then after that intervention he could have signed the finalised text in the end, once again. But I don't know what actually took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I understand it's very difficult for you to tell us. But if this was the brief procedure or, in other words, a directive coming directly from the supreme commander himself, if no inputs came from subordinate services, I imagine that it would be the typist of the supreme commander who would put his initials. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, not. This man begins [as interpreted] to the Logistics Support Sector. I don't know if you understand me. I don't exclude this possibility, but I'm simply reading the document as it is written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this man "belongs" to the Logistics Support Sector; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will try to re-mark the two documents which are already in evidence as P2145 and 2147. If there was a third one, you should figure that out during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And also 2148. We must have our first break now, and we will resume 4.25. And I would like to invite Mr. McCloskey to give us an estimation of the length of his examination-in-chief after the break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was told that you have used, up to now, four hours and thirteen minutes. There are three-quarters of an hour left. If my recollection is serving me well, you have indicated that you will use five hours. Yes. Is it possible to finish in this time or do you need some more time? I'm only concerned about the possibility for this witness to stay over the weekend, if that is necessary, because if you are getting more time, we should give the accused also additional time for his cross-examination, and there will be some re-examination probably, so that it is unlikely we can conclude the evidence of this witness this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that, and I hope I can get done this one section. In fact, we would have no objection to the witness -- in fact, I would prefer if the witness was allowed to go home on Friday and that we bring him back some time after his very important family engagement when he is available. As I mentioned to you, it's a very important engagement that he go to. It's the celebration of the anniversary of the death of his mother, I believe. And we are always available for him coming back, but I will try to finish up in this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, of course, we all have to bear that in mind. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has a proposal. If the witness's testimony has to be finished this week, we believe that he has either to be at home on Saturday or maybe he has to travel on Saturday. We are prepared to work on Friday, even to have an extended sitting on Friday if need may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Or perhaps tomorrow. We should consider that possibility as well. What is your position, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From here to get to Visegrad is a long trip. I think he needs to travel on Friday just to make sure. So -- but, of course, we should hear, of course, from the general on these points too. He's the person that should be able to offer the best ideas. But I hope to finish up in the next hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, I would like to ask you, sir. When does your travel back to your home take place, on which day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is 40 days after the death of my mother, and we mark that on Saturday at 10.00 in the morning in Visegrad. My family is already travelling today to be in Visegrad on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there were already arrangements made for your travel back. When will that happen? What is the schedule of this flight? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Witnesses and Victims Unit told me that on the 1st April there is a direct flight to Belgrade at 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And that is Friday of this week. In that case, we can't sit on Friday. This is not possible. We should consider the possibility of an extended sitting tomorrow, if everybody would be in agreement of that. But it's premature to discuss that at this stage. Mr. McCloskey, I learned that the loss of the markings had something to do with the technical equipment the witness has used. We have to redo it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have two exhibits that I'm told need to be redone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I've been informed that there are two exhibits that need to be redone. The first one is 65 ter 5137, which was given the number P2147. And it should be the first page. And I believe it's the now famous "za" that we've done twice before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need only the B/C/S version enlarged on the screen, and the Court Usher should assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document with the marking should now be saved and is already in evidence as ... and I would like to ask the Court Officer. I think it's P2147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm told the next one is the same 5137 but the second page. And if we could blow that up. This one, I think we'll recall that the general had the original in his hands. And if he could again - thank you, General - circle General Mladic's initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Be patient, please. One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These markings -- this marking on this document will be the Exhibit P2145, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to correct myself. It's 2148.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to P1214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify if the markings on the document 2144 are saved. These were the initials of Mr. Tolimir and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be checked by the Registrar. I was told they are saved. It's not necessary to repeat that again. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, we need to go to the last page in the B/C/S. This with a slight reversal, though -- yes, if we could go over to the last page, page 24 in e-court. Sorry, it's the next -- it's page 24. Okay. We've got the Serbian correct. And now we just need to go to the English. It's page 1 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, just to try to see if I can help with Judge Mindua's questions about this: The directive itself was dated 8th of March, 1995, but this cover letter, being sent to the 1st Krajina Corps, is dated 17 March 1995. If the system is working as it should, will the copy of the directive that's being sent along with this cover letter be the final copy, the final version, of Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A directive sent to the corps commands is its final version, the final version of that directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see the corps commands getting this directive. The assistant commanders at the Main Staff that took part in the drafting of the directive - we've already seen that General Miletic had one - should the other assistant commanders have also had a copy of the final version?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was forwarded to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't -- you know, I know you weren't in their offices. That's not what I mean. But if the system is working as it should, should the assistant commanders that took part in putting the material in for this directive receive a final copy, as we know General Miletic did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that his copy was forwarded to him. Maybe he has kept the draft that he participated in putting together, but he was not supposed to get it; he was not supposed to be forwarded it, that directive. It should have been sent to the chiefs of sectors and independent administrations rather than to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So leaving General Miletic out and what version he may have had in the strong-box, did you say that the directive should have been sent to the other assistant commanders or should not have been sent to the other assistant commanders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commanders and chiefs of sectors should be copied with the directive because they should be aware of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, as to whether those copies were sent to them or not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course. All right. Can we go to 65 ter 1815.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see, General, in looking at this, that there's a receipt -- I believe it's a receipt stamp from the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade up in the right-hand corner. It's dated 1 July 1995; the document is, that is. And it's listed as, "To the Commands of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and Drina Corps." And I'm sure you'll agree with me that the Zvornik Brigade was a member of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a, as we see, a list of approved convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page in the B/C/S so the general can see whose name is at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a teletype, so we don't see a signature. Could we go to the -- we just need to move it over so we can see the name of the person that wrote it in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A bit further, please. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you -- we see this going out under the name of your boss. You weren't there at the time. And you'll remember you being asked about this in the previous trial, and you perhaps have had a chance to review it. We notice that it's in handwritten --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the first page of the B/C/S and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that it's -- under the date stamp is handwritten "Security organ." Now, if that was written in by the Zvornik Brigade, which I believe it was, can you offer us your views on what, if anything, about this document would have caused it to be of concern or sent to the security organ of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was it that governed the commander of the Zvornik Brigade to send a copy to the security organ. Maybe this is a copy of the original document. But there's nothing there. It says here "Approved." It says: "We inform that we have approved the movement of the following UNPROFOR convoys:" And there is a list of those convoys there. In any case, the brigade commander believed that his security organ has to be appraised of the contents. Maybe he wanted him to follow and monitor the passage of those convoys. I don't know what governed him, as I say, but this may be an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's look at -- it's page 3 of the English, and it should be page 1 of the B/C/S, and it's after the -- it's within the number 6. In fact, it's probably the next page, because it's just after the number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it starts with -- and I hope I've got it for you now. I know that's a bit small to look at. And General Miletic said to the addressees: "Note: The movement of the convoys under items 5 and 6 above, which has been approved conditionally, should be specially controlled by teams at check-points and liaison officers of the Drina Corps Command. Before they enter the territory of Republika Srpska on their return from Zagreb, check the cargo in the six lorries. It has been agreed that the six lorries will transport humanitarian aid for Zvornik and the same number of lorries should bring humanitarian aid to Sarajevo, to the Muslims. If the lorries come to Zvornik without the said cargo, do not let them go to Sarajevo or Srebrenica." And he goes on to say: "In other words, when the convoy arrives in Zvornik, check it, establish what it is carrying, and inform the commander, after which instructions regarding continuation of their journey will be given. "Inform about this only the men who deal with such issues and use the details for internal purposes only. Do not reveal them to third persons." And if we look at 5 and 6, what they're talking about, I won't go -- go read it all, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are referring to item 5 and 6? That should be on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. We should -- everyone should be able to go look at 5 and 6 so we can see what this paragraph is referring to. Thank you, Mr. President. We do see that 5 has to do with from Srebrenica through Bratunac, Zelinje, Drinjaca, Zvornik, Karakaj, Belgrade, and Zagreb, to rotate medical staff. A minibus, then personal equipment, mail bags. Then the next one is from Srebrenica to Zagreb along the same route, personal equipment, luggage, jeeps, lorries, people, personal weapons, rations. And I'm not so interested in the actual specifics of this; I think it speaks for itself. But we here -- we see here that General Miletic has made special care to actually repeat twice what he wants to happen to this convoy. Is that something that you were aware of that sometimes General Miletic would engage in when he's communicating with the people that are going to be receiving these convoys?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, he informs and provides instructions based on a decision by the commander. When requests reached them, before they wrote this document, they had to analyse those convoys, their routes and points of entry into the territory of the Republika Srpska, and the passage through the zone of responsibility of the VRS. What governed them, what kind of analysis they had, I don't know. I don't know anything about these specific instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I don't want to ask you about those specific instructions, just the process, so thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter -- and I should offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 1815 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2149 [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to 65 ter 4049.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, I know this is dated the 14th of July - you're not quite back yet - from the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, which we know is the Rogatica Brigade, to the Main Staff, personally to General Miletic, and titled "Protection of TVP," which is "Secret Military Information." And it's General Tolimir asking about getting radio sets with the KZU 63, which you've spoken of earlier, that gives crypto-protection to voice communications. Would dealing with this kind of matter, General Tolimir, fit within his job as assistant commander for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of data protection. That's one of the tasks of the Security Service, and this is carried out by the communications bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is operational security -- security and secrecy of a military operation, does that also fit in with General Tolimir's duties? I mean generally.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, security organs deal with protection and security at all levels, in all commands, at all levels, in all units. That's how their organs branch out to the battalion commands. In battalions, there are also officers who deal with security. As for operative organs, they design keys for communications devices. Those are code books which are temporary and valid for a certain period of time in a certain area where radio communications are used. The radio set 2/2K, this is used by detachments, but they are also fitted with an encryption device for data protection or to protect messages, voice messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document after I offer this one into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2950 [sic], Your Honours. Just to correct the transcript, it's 2150 [sic]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So 65 ter 4860.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have talked to us about the assistant commanders, General Miletic's job, the job of someone that Mladic would appoint to take over his duties, who can issue orders in various situations. And this is a document I'm sure you'll remember that we talked about before, and I think you can see the whole document on your screen. We can see that it's from the Main Staff on 21 July, marked "Very Urgent," regarding the dispatch of the Krajina -- of a Krajina unit from the Zvornik area to the Trnovo front. And if we could go to the next page in English, we'll see that it went out under the name of General Miletic. And we can clearly see, if we go back to the first page in English, that this is an order, and it says : "I order ..." And this is the 21st now. You've been back for four days. Do you recall this document? We see it has that "03/4" number, the strictly confidential number that you've told us was the Security Branch number. Do you have any memory aside from our last discussion a few years ago over this document? Do you remember if you saw it at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document 03/4 is part of my operative department. It is recorded in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember it at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this document from that time, but I can see that it was registered in the log-book of the Operative Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
